introduction-text: This is the place where you get to put the universe in your own hands. Here, everything revolves around stars, planets, and black holes, but in a way that lets you discover, experiment, and play for yourself.

In this interactive simulator, you step into the role of an astronomer and explore what happens when stars are born, evolve, and influence each other. Star Workshop lets you experiment with processes that, in the real universe, take millions of years. By playing with the properties of stars yourself, you discover just how complex and fascinating single and binary stars can be.
• Build your own star - see how it swells up, loses mass, and changes over time,
• Play with the life story of a single star - try out how a star can end up as a white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole
• Watch stars evolve in time - See stars swell up, cool down, lose mass, and interact with companions. What happens if one star gets so big it touches the other?
• Create your own binary star - Put two stars in orbit around each other. Experiment with orbit size and eccentricity (how round or stretched out an orbit is), and watch how their dance changes.
• Test 'what if?' scenarios - What if the star was twice as massive? What if the star lives in a binary instead of alone? What happens when stars get too close to each other?
• See what happens to planets like Earth - Find out if, and when, a star can eat a planet – and what can go wrong along the way
Start the Star Workshop and dive into the cosmos!

Behind Star Workshop runs the same kind of computer code that real astronomers use to study stars and binary systems — but you don’t see the code, you get to play with the results. On this website, you change a slider, run the simulation, and see the universe react. Under the hood, you’re controlling serious stellar evolution software; on the screen, you just click, drag, and explore — like a game, but powered by real physics, so you’re using real science without needing to code.
introduction-text2: Star Workshop is designed for everyone who is curious about the universe – you don’t need to be an expert, just a bit interested (and maybe brave enough to play with supernovae and black holes). Ready to discover the rules of the universe – and sometimes bend them a little?

Especially for high school students and their teachers, we offer assignments and research ideas that let you explore topics from the physics curriculum (such as gravity, energy, radiation, and the use of models) in a new way. With the simulators you can set up your own experiments, collect data, and make connections – for example for class projects or final research papers. We are also developing a more extensive teaching package around Star Workshop , so that teachers can integrate the material into their lessons even more easily.
This website was developed by Evert Rol and Silvia Toonen as part of the outreach project Sterrenstrijd. For questions, comments, or more information, you can contact us at toonen at uva.nl.
introduction-text-star: Here, you can explore the life story of a star: from its birth on the main sequence all the way to its final state as a white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole. You can set the mass anywhere between about 0.01 and 100 times the mass of the Sun, adjust the metallicity (= metal content), and choose how long you want to follow the evolution.

For reference: our Sun has (by definition) a mass of 1 Solar mass, a metallicity of about 0.02, and an age of roughly 4.6 billion years. The universe itself is about 13.8 billion years old. Stars that formed when the universe was young often have a lower metallicity .
introduction-text-binary: Here you can explore the life cycle of a binary star system: two stars orbiting each other and shaping each other’s future. This time you set not one, but two stellar masses, as well as the metallicity (= metal content) and the timespan of the evolution, just like in the single-star simulator.

In addition, you can define the orbit of the system: the orbital separation (how far apart the stars are on average) and the eccentricity (how circular or elongated the orbit is). This lets you see how close the stars get to each other, when they start to interact, transfer mass, or even merge, and under which conditions supernovae, compact binaries, or black hole pairs can form.

What about planets? You simulate those with the same binary simulator: choose Planet as the Companion and enter the mass of the planet in Earth masses (from 0.05 Earth masses to 100 Jupiter masses). With the orbital separation you set how close the planet is, and you can see whether, and when, the star swells up and swallows the planet.
mass-tooltip: Initial mass of the star in Solar mass
mass1-tooltip: Mass of the primary star in Solar mass; this should be larger than or equal to the secondary star.
mass2-tooltip: Mass of the secondary star in Solar mass; this should be smaller than or equal to the primary star.
mass2p-tooltip: Mass of the planet in Earth masses. The Earth has 1 Earth mass, Jupiter about 318.
ecc-tooltip: Eccentricity of the elliptical orbit: 0 is completely circular, 0.99 is nearly a straight line.
sep-tooltip: Separation between the two stars, in Solar radii.
periodin-tooltip: How long the two stars take to go around each other once, in days. The simulator turns this into a separation using the two masses.
time-tooltip: Time span of simulation in units of mega-years (= million years)
metal-tooltip: Metalliticity is the fraction of atoms with atom numbers higher than Helium compared to the total star mass (which is mainly Hydrogen and Helium)
update-directly-tooltip: Run SeBa near instantly when changing any of the input parameters
efftemp-field: effective temperature of the star (unit: Kelvin)
lum-field: luminosity of the star (unit: Solar luminosity)
mass1-field: stellar mass of star 1 (unit: Solar mass)
radius1-field: stellar radius of star 1 (unit: Solar radii)
coremass1-field: core mass of star 1 (unit: Solar mass)
mass2-field: stellar mass of star 2 (unit: Solar mass)
radius2-field: stellar radius of star 2 (unit: Solar radii)
coremass2-field: core mass of star 2 (unit: Solar mass)
movie-aria: Animation of the evolution of your star
movie-empty: Press start to watch your star's life
movie-caption: The movie shows your star: its size is on a logarithmic scale and its colour follows the surface temperature. Time is also logarithmic and slows down when the star changes a lot. The dashed ring is as big as the Sun. The “Download movie” button saves the movie as a video file. Recording takes as long as the movie itself; keep this tab open.
movie-credit: Supernova remnant: the Crab Nebula. Image: NASA, ESA, J. Hester and A. Loll (Arizona State University).
movie-credit-helix: Planetary nebula: the Helix Nebula (NGC 7293). Image: NASA, ESA, and C.R. O'Dell (Vanderbilt University).
movie-credit-helix-short: Helix Nebula: NASA, ESA, C.R. O'Dell (Vanderbilt)
movie-credit-short: Crab Nebula: NASA, ESA, J. Hester and A. Loll (ASU)
graph-caption-single: The graph shows how the properties of your star change. “Quick pick” gives you a ready-made graph, such as the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, or you can choose what goes on the axes yourself. The colour of the line is the phase of the star (see the legend), and the white dot shows where the movie is now. Hover over the line for the exact values. “Download graph” saves the graph as a picture with a white background.
graph-caption-binary: The graph shows how the properties of your stars change. Choose what goes on the axes and whether they are linear or logarithmic. Star 1 and star 2 have their own options. The colour of the line shows whether the stars interact (see the legend), and the white dot shows where the movie is now. Hover over the line for the exact values. “Download graph” saves the graph as a picture with a white background.
download-data-note: “CSV for Excel” uses semicolons and decimal commas, so that Excel with Dutch settings shows the columns correctly. Use the plain “CSV” for Python, R and other programs, or for Excel with English settings.
movie-caption-binary: The movie shows your binary: the two stars orbit each other. When a star is big, its size and its distance to the other star are to scale; small stars are drawn larger than they are, otherwise you would not see them. The colour follows the surface temperature. When a star becomes so big that gas flows to the other star, you see that stream of gas: this is mass transfer. Time is also logarithmic and slows down when a lot happens. The “Download movie” button saves the movie as a video file. Recording takes as long as the movie itself; keep this tab open.
